title: Polynomial Rödl, Virality and Erdős–Hajnal Equivalence

items.title: The polynomial Rödl property for a finite forbidden family
The viral property for a finite forbidden family
Many good $2t$-vertex subsets force many homogeneous $k$-sets
items.strategy: Use the Bucić–Fox–Pham / Nguyen double-counting step. Count incidences between homogeneous $k$-sets and $2t$-vertex subsets; every good $2t$-set contributes at least one homogeneous $k$-set because it contains a $t$-vertex induced subgraph in the hereditary class, and every graph in that class has the $(t,k)$-homogeneous property.

items.title: Small total induced-copy expectation forces many homogeneous $k$-sets
items.strategy: Package the family version of the sampling lemma. If a random $2t$-vertex subset has expected total forbidden-copy count at most $t/2$, Markov makes at least half of those subsets good; deleting one vertex from each forbidden copy leaves a $t$-vertex family-free induced subgraph, so the previous lemma yields many homogeneous $k$-sets.

items.title: Without a large $\epsilon$-sparse induced subgraph, the number of $k$-vertex stable sets is bounded
items.strategy: Follow Nguyen's Kleitman–Winston style induction. A stable $k$-set either contains a chosen high-degree vertex or avoids it; recurse on the non-neighbour set in the first case and on the deleted graph in the second, using the no-large-sparse-set hypothesis to keep the parameters admissible.

items.title: Every finite family with the Erdős–Hajnal property is viral
items.strategy: Handle the vacuous $K_0$ and $K_1$ cases first. Otherwise take an Erdős–Hajnal exponent $c$, choose an integer $m$ with $mc\ge1$, set $t=k^m$, and use the family-free class to guarantee that every good $t$-vertex induced subgraph contains a homogeneous $k$-set. Bound the expected forbidden-copy count in a random $2t$-vertex subset by linearity of expectation, get many homogeneous $k$-sets from the sampling lemma, and then apply the stable-set counting lemma to $G$ and to $\overline G$ to contradict the absence of an $\epsilon$-restricted linear subset.

items.title: The viral property implies the polynomial Rödl property
items.strategy: If a graph is $\mathcal H$-free, then every forbidden induced-copy count is zero, so the viral hypothesis applies with no extra work.

items.title: The polynomial Rödl property implies the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Let $d$ witness the polynomial Rödl property. For large $n$, choose $\epsilon=n^{-1/(d+1)}$ and take the restricted set $X$ of size at least $n^{1/(d+1)}$; if $X$ is sparse, greedy colouring of $G[X]$ gives a stable set of size at least $1/(2\epsilon)$, and if $X$ is dense the same bound in the complement gives a clique. A finite small-order check closes the remaining values of $n$.

items.title: For a finite family, the Erdős–Hajnal property, the polynomial Rödl property, and virality are equivalent
items.strategy: Combine the previous theorem and corollaries to close the cycle Erdős–Hajnal $\Rightarrow$ viral $\Rightarrow$ polynomial Rödl $\Rightarrow$ Erdős–Hajnal.

items.title: For a single graph, the Erdős–Hajnal property, the polynomial Rödl property, and virality are equivalent
items.strategy: Apply the finite-family theorem to the singleton family $\{H\}$, using that $\{H\}$-free means $H$-free.

title: Polynomial Rödl, Virality and Erdős–Hajnal Equivalence — Examples

items.title: The singleton family $\{P_3\}$ is viral
items.strategy: The published three-vertex classification gives the Erdős–Hajnal property for $P_3$, and the new singleton equivalence turns that immediately into the viral property.

items.title: A family containing $K_1$ is viral for vacuous reasons
items.strategy: For every nonempty graph $G$, the labelled induced-copy count of $K_1$ is exactly $|V(G)|$, so for every $\epsilon<1$ the inequality $\operatorname{ind}_{K_1}(G)<(\epsilon^d|V(G)|)^1$ never holds. The viral implication therefore has no instances to check.

items.title: The polynomial Rödl witness need not be the whole graph
items.strategy: Use the disjoint union of two equal cliques, which is $P_3$-free and therefore lies in a polynomial Rödl family by the singleton equivalence. The whole graph has about half the vertices adjacent to each vertex and about half nonadjacent, so for every fixed $\epsilon<1/2$ it is neither $\epsilon$-sparse nor $\epsilon$-dense, even though one clique side is a $0$-dense restricted set.

items.title: The empty forbidden family is not Erdős–Hajnal
items.strategy: For the empty family, every graph is vacuously family-free, so its free class is the class of all finite graphs. The published random-graph corollary shows that class is not Erdős–Hajnal, so the empty family cannot satisfy any of the equivalent properties.
